ingredients.name: Whole green mung beans (mung ata)
ingredients.notes: about 1 cup; soaked overnight or for at least 6-8 hours; drain before cooking. Sprouted mung beans can also be used and require less cooking time.

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: enough to cover the mung beans; add more during cooking if needed

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.notes: added once the mung beans are fully tender

ingredients.name: Lime
ingredients.notes: juiced; optional, added at the end

steps.instruction: Soak the mung beans in plenty of cold water overnight or for at least 6-8 hours. Drain and rinse well before use.
Heat coconut oil in a pan over medium heat. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add cumin seeds, fenugreek, curry leaves, pandan leaf, and cinnamon stick. Sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion, garlic, and green chillies. Cook until the onion softens and turns lightly golden, about 4-5 minutes.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, and curry powder. Stir briefly. Add the chopped tomato and cook for 2 minutes.

Add the soaked and drained mung beans. Stir to coat well with the spice base. Add the water and salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce to medium-low heat, cover, and cook for 20-25 minutes until the mung beans are completely tender and beginning to split. Check occasionally and add more water if the pan dries out before the beans are cooked.
Pour in the thick coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer uncovered for 3-5 minutes over low heat until the gravy thickens. Squeeze in lime juice if using. Taste and adjust salt.
Serve hot with rice, hoppers, or string hoppers. This is a particularly good pairing with plain hoppers or pittu for breakfast.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against foodcnr.com, hungrylankan.com, topsrilankanrecipe.com, loveandotherspices.com, and infolanka.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources; strong agreement on overnight soak, the full-temper technique, and coconut milk added only once the beans are fully tender
notes: Mung bean curry (mung ata maluwa) is one of the most nutritionally valued everyday curries in Sri Lanka, eaten across all communities and considered gentle enough for children, the elderly, and those recovering from illness. Unlike red lentil dhal (sl_015) which breaks down completely into a smooth soup, mung beans hold their shape even when fully tender, giving the curry a heartier, more toothsome texture. The overnight soak is important for reducing cooking time and improving digestibility -- un-soaked mung beans take significantly longer to cook and can cause more gas. Sprouted mung beans (germs are visible) are an increasingly popular variant used by health-conscious home cooks; they require only 10-15 minutes of cooking rather than 20-25. The total_time_min of 510 minutes reflects the 8-hour overnight soak.
